extracted.intended_audience: experimental scientists, laboratory physicists, and advanced students learning experimental method and measurement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and conducting physical experiments to measure quantitative phenomena accurately by identifying, minimizing, compensating for, or correcting interfering causes of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-observation limitation / necessity of multiple observations
rubrics_metrics.description: The general principle is that a single observation can render known only a single quantity; hence, if several different quantitative effects are known to enter into any investigation, we must have at least as many distinct observations as there are quantities to be determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every complete experiment will consist in general of several operations. Guided, if possible, by previous knowledge of the causes in action, arrange determinations so that by a simple mathematical process the separate quantities may be distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The physicist may seek for some special mode of experiment or opportunity of observation, in which the error is non-existent or inappreciable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: astronomers observing objects on the meridian or near the zenith to minimise atmospheric refraction; placing clocks in cellars to eliminate temperature variation; using ice (Davy) to prevent conduction of heat; surrounding a thermometer with a copper cylinder adjusted to air temperature (Joule). Reduce source of variation first before applying other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Find opportunities of observation when all interfering phenomena remain constant, and only the subject of observation is at one time present and another time absent; the difference between two observations then gives its amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when relative difference is needed rather than absolute value. Examples: differential observation of nearby stars to detect parallax; transit observations (Venus) where refraction affects both object and reference equally; Leslie's differential thermometer; substitutive weighing and micrometer-equipped telescopes. Useful when interfering phenomena affect both measurements equally so they cancel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the amount of the interfering effect by the best available mode and then make a corresponding correction in the results of observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: temperature corrections for barometer readings using known dilatation coefficients of mercury; capillarity corrections for narrow tubes; determining friction by separate experiments (e.g., Smeaton's method, Joule's repeat without condensation to measure friction heat); Regnault's use of two calorimeters to tabulate and apply corrections. Where corrections can be calculated reliably, tabulate them for general use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invent some mode of neutralising the interfering cause by balancing against it an exactly equal and opposite cause of unknown amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when the error varies and cannot be practicably calculated. Examples: attach a dummy sealed glass globe to the opposite scale to cancel buoyant air effects; connect two equally magnetised needles in opposite directions (astatic) in galvanometers; Faraday's paired-tube torsion balance to compare gases so envelope and ambient magnetism cancel. Design apparatus so the disturbing forces act equally and oppositely on matched parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct the experiment so that the interfering cause may act in opposite directions in alternate observations, the mean result being free from interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternating observations with reversed conditions to cancel systematic biases. (Page presents this method as one of the five principal methods; specific apparatus examples are implied by practices like reversing orientation or switching roles of matched components.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Make primary effect large relative to interfering effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If full avoidance is impossible, make the effect to be measured as considerable as possible compared with the other effects, which are reduced to a minimum and treated as noxious errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: In rudimentary experiments it may be preferable to arrange conditions so interfering errors are all negative (Grove's magnetisation experiment kept electromagnet cooler so it would cool rather than warm the iron), ensuring measured effect is a lower bound rather than spuriously large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use test experiments to quantify apparatus- or observer-specific errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform operations not intended to give the principal quantity but to measure quantities which would otherwise remain as errors in the result (test experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: determine personal error by making an artificial star move and recording its passage electrically; train observers with mechanical models (Transit of Venus expeditions); measure friction by repeating runs without the main effect to quantify heat from friction. Test experiments allow separate determination of biases and apparatus-specific corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce errors by averaging and distribution of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase the number of observations and distribute them so that, in the final mean, as much error in one way is as in the other; this reduces random or bidirectional instrumental errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used widely in astronomy and other fields: by taking many observations under varied conditions, random variations tend to cancel in the mean. Note: does not remove errors that are unidirectional (personal error) unless specifically addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for and control 'personal error' of observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal error (inclination to record events a little too soon or late) affects all observations in the same direction and to the same average amount and cannot be eliminated by mere averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine personal error absolutely by test experiments (artificial star with electrical timing), compare judgments among observers, and train observers (mechanical models) to reduce systematic biases. Recognise magnitude (fractions of a second) and correct or calibrate accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design standards and instruments with comparable calibration conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use instruments under circumstances of position and temperature exactly similar to those in which they were graduated; make standards defined at fixed temperatures where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: thermometer reads differently when laid flat vs vertical or if recently heated; standard bars should be defined at the same uniform temperature (e.g., freezing point) to allow direct comparison; account for material-dependent expansion when comparing national standards (metre vs yard). Avoid inferring from one bar to another due to differing molecular conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise environmental heat/radiation losses and use symmetric procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Because heat is difficult to confine, reduce losses by insulation and, where possible, employ symmetric procedures so losses reciprocally balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use double-sided calorimeters, bright surfaces, and insulating materials (swans-down wool); Rumford's idea to start calorimeter colder than air so gain then loss approximately balance (but note Regnault's critique that gains and losses don't follow identical laws). For highest accuracy, use alternating identical apparatus to measure corrections (Regnault).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware limits of ostensibly elegant methods and evaluate net error effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An ingenious method that seems to remove one error may introduce other errors, sometimes larger than those removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Huyghens' cycloidal pendulum isochronism introduces mechanical complications that add error; Foucault's pendulum demonstrates Earth's rotation but cannot measure it exactly due to lateral motions producing elliptic paths that may overpower the rotation signal; Gay-Lussac's siphon-barometer idea fails because surfaces become sullied and capillarity differs. Always check whether an improvement's practical implementation degrades overall accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When corrections are tedious, prefer compensating designs to avoid routine correction labour
rubrics_metrics.description: If calculating corrections for every measurement is excessively laborious (e.g., air buoyancy corrections in frequent weighings), devise apparatus that makes the correction constant or self-cancelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: chemists attach a dummy sealed globe of equal capacity so the buoyancy correction is the same for both and may be neglected; choose design solutions to save repeated calculation when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use matching/duplicate apparatus and alternation to determine and apply corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ two identical instruments or setups alternately so that one measures the main effect while the other determines corrections; alternation gives data to correct the primary readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regnault's use of two calorimeters alternately is cited: while one measures the latent heat, the other determines corrections for radiation/conduction and pipe heat. This yields higher accuracy than single-apparatus correction estimates.
